title: Salah al-Din
hookLine: the Kurdish sultan who united Egypt and Syria

cards: As if he were being driven to his death. That, in one account, is how a young officer later described riding with his uncle's army to Egypt. He hadn't wanted to go.

His name was Yusuf, son of Ayyub, from a Kurdish family that served the Turkish ruler of Syria, Nur al-Din. He would become known by an honorific, a title of praise: Salah al-Din, the righteousness of the faith.
Some in the west learned to call him Saladin. The reluctant officer would spend his life on yesterday's problem: a divided people.

teach.b: In Egypt, the Fatimid caliphs still ruled from Cairo, the city you met earlier this month. Salah al-Din's uncle became their vizier and soon died, and the post passed to the young Yusuf.
Then he did something quiet and enormous: he had the Friday sermon in Egypt said in the name of the Sunni caliph, the Abbasid in Baghdad, not the Fatimid one. The Fatimid line came to an end.
When Nur al-Din died, Salah al-Din moved into Syria and, over years of bargaining and battle, brought Damascus, Aleppo and other cities under his rule.

teach.h: EGYPT AND SYRIA UNDER ONE RULER.
teach.b: Now Egypt and Syria answered to one ruler. Not everyone welcomed him. Some of Nur al-Din's family and followers saw a servant taking his master's lands, and said so.
His biographer, the judge Ibn Shaddad, who served beside him, paints a man who prayed, listened to hadith read aloud, wept easily, and gave away so much that he left almost nothing at his death.

Biographers can love their subjects, so it's fair to hold that portrait a little loosely. Whatever else drove him, the work of his life, as these sources tell it, was bringing divided lands under one rule.
The Qur'an has a line for that hope.

teach.h: HOLD FAST, ALL OF YOU TOGETHER.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A Kurdish officer, serving a Turkish lord, uniting Arab lands.

how: Salah al-Din's tomb in Damascus is still visited, and Ibn Shaddad's biography of him is still read.

games.q: you're the young Yusuf, vizier in Fatimid Cairo, serving Nur al-Din, who looks to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. what do you do?
o: keep the Friday sermon in the Fatimid caliph's name.
have the sermon said in the Abbasid caliph's name.
games.why: he had the sermon said for the Abbasid caliph. it was quiet, and it ended Fatimid rule in Egypt.

practice: Bring to mind one place where people you belong to are divided, a family that has stopped talking, friends on two sides of a quarrel, and without trying to solve it, see what they still share.

Then ask what small thing could bring two of them a little closer, without forcing anyone. If you pray, you can say the line, hold fast, all of you together; if you don't, simply picture them together.

wordCard.voice: Salah al-Din. Yusuf, son of Ayyub, the Kurdish officer who ended Fatimid rule in Egypt and united Egypt and Syria. His title means the righteousness of the faith. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the righteousness of the faith; an honorific title. His own name was Yusuf.

carryVoice: Your line: the kurdish sultan. Uniting was slow work, city by city. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

sources.q: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.
